sections.title: The Gateway: How did humans teach wood, skin, metal and air to sing?
sections.html:
Web address: /instruments/how-instruments-sing/ · Keywords: musical instruments, how instruments work, types of musical instruments, Indian musical instruments, instruments for beginners

A hollow bone, a stretched skin, a twisted gut string, a bent sheet of brass. None of these is music on its own. Yet humans have found ways to make every one of them sing, cry, thunder and laugh. There are thousands of instruments on Earth, and every culture has its own.

This short course asks one big question in seven steps: what is a musical instrument, and how does it turn a material into music? It goes from Ice Age bone flutes to the sitar's buzz, from the Natyashastra's four classes to the synthesizer, and ends with advice on choosing your own first instrument. Each page takes about two minutes.

By the end you will be able to:

  • Name the four ways (five, with electricity) that instruments make sound.
  • Explain why a string or an air column gives a definite note.
  • Say why two instruments sound different on the same note.
  • Compare the Indian and the European ways of classifying instruments.
  • Choose a first instrument with good reasons.

sections.title: What is the oldest instrument ever found?
sections.html:
Short answer: The oldest certain instruments are flutes made of bird bone and mammoth ivory from caves in south-west Germany, about 40,000 to 43,000 years old. A 50,000-year-old bone from Slovenia may be a Neanderthal flute, but scientists still argue about it.

Keywords: oldest musical instrument, oldest flute, Hohle Fels flute, Divje Babe flute, prehistoric music

The flutes of the Swabian Jura

In 2008 archaeologists in the Hohle Fels cave found a flute carved from the wing bone of a griffon vulture, with five finger holes and a notched end. Pieces of ivory and bone flutes also came from nearby Geissenklösterle and Vogelherd. Radiocarbon dating puts them at about 40,000 to 43,000 years old (Conard and colleagues, Nature, 2009; Higham and colleagues, 2012). Making an ivory flute meant splitting a tusk, hollowing both halves and gluing them airtight: these were skilled makers.

The Divje Babe puzzle

A cave bear's thigh bone with two round holes, found at Divje Babe in Slovenia in 1995, is about 50,000 to 60,000 years old. Its finder, Ivan Turk, argued it is a Neanderthal flute. Many other scientists think the holes are bite marks from a hyena or bear. The question is still open, which is itself worth learning: good science says "we are not sure" when it is not sure.

Instruments that left no trace

Clapping, stamping, rattles of seeds, drums of skin and wood rot away. So the first instruments were almost certainly older than any we have found. In India, rock shelters at Bhimbetka show dancers, and some granite boulders and temple pillars ring when struck, like the musical pillars of the Vittala temple at Hampi.

Remember this: The oldest instruments we can hold are flutes, but the first music was surely the voice and the body.

Next: A flute makes a note. But why does any instrument make a note at all, instead of just noise?

sections.title: Why does a guitar string make a note at all?
sections.html:
Short answer: A stretched string vibrates in a regular pattern, many times a second. A regular, repeating vibration is what our ears hear as a definite pitch. Its length, tension and weight set how fast it vibrates.

Keywords: how a string makes sound, frequency and pitch, standing waves, Mersenne's laws, physics of music

Noise and notes

Drop a bunch of keys and you get noise: a jumble of vibrations at random speeds. Pluck a string and you get a note, because it vibrates back and forth at one steady rate, called its frequency, measured in hertz (Hz: vibrations per second). The A above middle C is tuned to 440 Hz in most of the world today.

Three dials on every string

In 1636 the French friar Marin Mersenne wrote down three rules, now called Mersenne's laws:

  • Shorter string, higher note (press a guitar fret or a sitar string and you shorten it).
  • Tighter string, higher note (that is what tuning pegs do).
  • Lighter (thinner) string, higher note (so a bass guitar has thick strings).

Standing waves and overtones

A string fixed at both ends can only vibrate in whole patterns: the whole length, two halves, three thirds and so on. These are the fundamental and its overtones (harmonics), all sounding at once. The same idea works for air in a tube: a flute or a trumpet is a column of air vibrating in standing waves.

The body that makes it loud

A bare string is quiet. The wooden body of a guitar, the gourd of a sitar or the skin of a banjo picks up the vibration and moves much more air. That is called resonance.

Remember this: A note is a regular vibration; length, tension and weight are the three dials that set it.

sections.title: Why do a flute and a violin sound different on the same note?
sections.html:
Short answer: Because each instrument mixes its overtones in a different recipe and starts and ends its sound differently. This "colour" of a sound is called timbre (say TAM-ber).

Keywords: timbre, tone colour, overtones, harmonics, why instruments sound different

The recipe of overtones

Every real note is a chord in disguise: the fundamental plus many quieter overtones. A flute's sound has strong fundamental and few overtones, so it sounds pure and breathy. A violin's sound has a rich spread of overtones, so it sounds bright and full. A clarinet, because its tube behaves as if closed at one end, is strong in the odd-numbered harmonics, which gives its hollow, woody sound.

Attack, sustain, decay

Timbre is also about time. A piano note hits hard and fades away; a violin can grow louder in the middle of a note; a tabla stroke cracks and rings. Scientists call this the envelope. Cut the attack off a recorded piano note and many people cannot tell it is a piano.

Materials and players

Wood, metal, skin, gut, nylon and steel each colour the overtones. So does the player. Ustad Bismillah Khan and another shehnai player sound different on the same instrument because of breath, lips and taste.

An Indian discovery

In 1920 C. V. Raman showed that the Indian mridangam and tabla are unusual drums. Most drums give overtones that clash (they are "inharmonic"), so they sound like thumps. The black spot of paste on these drums (the syahi or soru) loads the skin so that its overtones line up almost like a string's. That is why the tabla can be tuned to the tonic Sa and "sings".

Remember this: Same note, different recipe: timbre is the mix and the timing of overtones.

sections.title: How did India classify instruments 2,000 years ago?
sections.html:
Short answer: The Natyashastra, a Sanskrit treatise on drama attributed to Bharata (compiled roughly between 200 BCE and 200 CE), sorts instruments into four classes by how they make sound: tata (strings), sushira (hollow, wind), avanaddha (covered, drums) and ghana (solid). Europe's modern system follows the same logic.

Keywords: Natyashastra instruments, tata sushira avanaddha ghana, classification of Indian instruments, Bharata Muni

The four classes

  • Tata vadya (stretched): instruments with strings, like the veena and sitar.
  • Sushira vadya (hollow): instruments played by blowing air, like the flute and shehnai.
  • Avanaddha vadya (covered): instruments with a skin stretched over them, like the mridangam and tabla.
  • Ghana vadya (solid): instruments that sound by themselves when struck, like cymbals, bells and the clay ghatam.

Why this was clever

Bharata did not sort instruments by what they look like, or by what region they come from. He sorted them by what vibrates: a string, air, a skin or the solid body. That rule works for any instrument in any country, even ones he never saw.

The link to Europe

In 1880 Victor-Charles Mahillon, curator of the instrument museum of the Brussels Conservatory, used four very similar classes for his catalogue. He knew the Indian system through instruments and writings sent to Brussels by the Bengali scholar Sourindro Mohun Tagore. In 1914 Erich von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs refined Mahillon's scheme into the system museums still use (INS-02). Other traditions have their own systems too: China's ancient bayin sorts instruments by eight materials (metal, stone, silk, bamboo, gourd, clay, skin and wood).

Remember this: String, air, skin, solid: India's four-fold system is the grandparent of the world's museum system.

sections.title: Why does a sitar buzz?
sections.html:
Short answer: The sitar's strings rest on a wide, gently curved bridge called the jawari. As each string vibrates it brushes the curve, which shortens and lengthens it many times a second and throws energy into high overtones. That gives the bright, shimmering buzz.

Keywords: sitar jawari, why sitar sounds like that, sympathetic strings, tanpura buzz, Indian string instruments

A bridge that touches back

On a guitar or violin the bridge is a sharp edge: the string leaves it at one point. On the sitar, tanpura, Saraswati veena and rudra veena, the bridge is a flat, slightly curved plate of bone, horn or wood. The string grazes it. Raman studied this too, in the early 1920s. Makers "open" the jawari by sanding the curve with great care; a good jawari is a sitar's soul.

Strings that play themselves

Under the main strings a sitar has eleven to thirteen thin taraf (sympathetic) strings, tuned to the notes of the raga. They are never plucked. When a main string sounds a note, the matching taraf string vibrates by itself, giving a halo of sound. The sarangi, the Norwegian hardanger fiddle and the Swedish nyckelharpa use the same trick.

Many instruments, one taste

The buzz is not an accident of one instrument. It is a taste shared across the subcontinent, and across Africa too: the kora's and mbira's buzzing rattles do a similar job. The point is to make each note rich and alive, to suit music that dwells long on single notes.

Remember this: The buzz is designed, not a fault: a curved bridge plus sympathetic strings make the sitar shimmer.

sections.title: How did electricity change instruments?
sections.html:
Short answer: Electricity let instruments make sound with no vibrating material of their own (the theremin, the synthesizer) and let quiet instruments become loud (the electric guitar). It added a fifth class, the electrophones, and later turned the computer into an instrument.

Keywords: electronic instruments history, theremin, electric guitar invention, Moog synthesizer, electrophones

Amplifying the old

Pickups turn a string's vibration into an electric signal that an amplifier makes loud. The Rickenbacker "Frying Pan" lap steel guitar (early 1930s) was among the first commercial electric guitars; the solid-body Fender Telecaster (1950) and Gibson Les Paul (1952) followed. Loudness changed music itself: rock, blues and Bollywood orchestras grew around it.

Making sound from nothing

The theremin (Leon Theremin, around 1920) is played without touch: the hands move near two antennas. The Moog synthesizer (Robert Moog, 1964) builds sound from electronic oscillators and filters. The Yamaha DX7 (1983) made digital synthesis cheap, and the MIDI standard (1983) let instruments and computers talk.

Machines that keep time and copy sound

The Roland TR-808 drum machine (1980) shaped hip-hop and pop. Samplers let any recorded sound become an instrument. In India, the electronic tanpura and tabla boxes became practice tools, and the Roland Octapad pads became a fixture of film-music percussion.

Today

A laptop, a phone app or an AI model can now be an instrument. Curt Sachs added the class "electrophones" in 1940; in 2011 the MIMO project revised it again.

Remember this: Electricity added a fifth way to sound: no string, air, skin or solid needed.

sections.title: Which instrument should you learn first?
sections.html:
Short answer: The one whose music you love most and will practise daily. For many beginners a keyboard, ukulele, recorder, bansuri or harmonium is a gentle start, because a note comes easily. Your own voice is the instrument many Indian gurus begin with.

Keywords: best first instrument, easiest instrument to learn, learn music beginner, which instrument for my child

Five questions to ask

  1. What music do you love? Love keeps you practising. A tabla lover will not stay with a violin.
  2. How fast do you want a pleasant sound? Keyboard, ukulele and harmonium are quick; violin, sarangi and the French horn are slow at first.
  3. Your body and age: small hands suit a ukulele or a quarter-size violin; children's teeth matter for brass.
  4. Budget and space: a recorder costs very little; a piano needs a room.
  5. Is there a teacher or a group? Learning with others helps most people.

The Indian way

Many Hindustani and Carnatic gurus ask students to sing first, because the voice teaches pitch and phrasing that every instrument needs. "Gayaki ang" (a singing style) is praised on the sitar and sarangi alike.

The honest truth

Every instrument becomes hard at a high level. Ten minutes of focused daily practice usually beats two hours once a week. Part 10 (INS-33) gives a fuller guide, with learning paths and buying tips.

Remember this: Pick by love, then by ease; practise a little every day.

sections.title: Recap: the story of instruments in one page
sections.html:
Short answer: Instruments turn vibration into music. They make sound in four ancient ways (string, air, skin, solid) and one modern way (electricity). From 40,000-year-old flutes to synthesizers, every culture has built its own, and India gave the world its first lasting classification.

Keywords: musical instruments summary, history of instruments, types of instruments explained

  1. Body and voice came first: clapping, stamping, singing.
  2. Bone flutes (about 40,000 years ago) are the oldest instruments found.
  3. Ancient civilisations: harps and lyres of Ur (about 2500 BCE), the Chinese bells of Marquis Yi (433 BCE), the vina of ancient India.
  4. Classification: the Natyashastra's four classes; China's eight materials; Hornbostel–Sachs (1914).
  5. The great inventions: the violin family (Cremona, 16th century), the piano (Cristofori, around 1700), the saxophone (1840s), the drum kit (early 1900s).
  6. Electricity: theremin, electric guitar, synthesizer, drum machine, computer.
  7. Today: thousands of instruments, many at risk, many being revived; the choice of your first one is yours.

Remember this: Every instrument is a human idea about how to make a material sing.

Next: Part 1 sets out the two great classification systems side by side.

parts.title: How Instruments Are Classified
parts.intro: About this Part. Before the families, the two great maps: India's ancient four-fold system and the Hornbostel–Sachs system used by museums worldwide. A third, China's eight materials, is added for comparison. Every instrument in this booklet carries both labels.

sections.title: The Indian system: the four vadyas of the Natyashastra
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-01. The Natyashastra (chapters 28 to 34 deal with music) is attributed to the sage Bharata and was compiled roughly between 200 BCE and 200 CE. Later texts such as Sharngadeva's Sangita Ratnakara (13th century) kept the four classes and described many more instruments. See also: MUS-01, MUS-22.1, INS-00.04.
  • INS-01.1 Tata vadya (stringed): any instrument whose sound comes from a stretched string, plucked, bowed or struck: veena, sitar, sarod, sarangi, santoor, violin, guitar.
  • INS-01.2 Sushira vadya (hollow, wind): instruments sounded by a column of air: bansuri, shehnai, nadaswaram, shankh (conch), harmonium (by later writers), trumpet.
  • INS-01.3 Avanaddha vadya (covered, membrane): drums with a skin stretched over a frame or shell: mridangam, pakhawaj, tabla, dholak, nagara, damaru, chenda. Bharata names the pushkara drums (mridanga, panava, dardura) as the most important.
  • INS-01.4 Ghana vadya (solid): instruments that vibrate as one solid body: cymbals (manjira, tala), bells (ghanta), gongs, the clay ghatam, the jal tarang, the wooden khartal and the morchang (jaw harp).
  • INS-01.5 Sharira vina, the body as instrument: Indian texts call the human voice the gatra vina or sharira vina (the body-veena) and treat it as the model for all instruments (see INS-00.07).
  • INS-01.6 Later Indian refinements: the Sangita Ratnakara and later treatises sub-divided each class (for example, drums by shape and stroke; strings by plucking or bowing). Modern Indian scholars such as B. C. Deva (Musical Instruments of India, 1978) mapped the old classes onto the Hornbostel–Sachs numbers.

sections.title: The Hornbostel–Sachs system (1914, revised 2011)
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-02. Erich Moritz von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs published Systematik der Musikinstrumente in the Zeitschrift für Ethnologie in 1914, building on Victor-Charles Mahillon's Brussels catalogue (1880). It uses decimal numbers, like a library: the more digits, the more exact the class. Sachs added electrophones in 1940. The MIMO (Musical Instrument Museums Online) consortium published a revised version in 2011. See also: INS-03 (how the systems match).

  • 11 Struck idiophones: hit directly or indirectly: cymbals, gongs, bells, xylophones, the ghatam, castanets, the steelpan, the cajón.
  • 12 Plucked idiophones (lamellophones): a tongue of metal or wood is plucked: the jaw harp (morchang), the mbira and kalimba, the music box.
  • 13 Friction idiophones: rubbed: the glass harmonica, the musical saw, the singing bowl when rubbed.
  • 14 Blown idiophones: the air makes a solid vibrate (rare): the aeolsklavier.

  • 21 Struck drums: by hand or stick: tabla, mridangam, djembe, timpani, the drum kit. Sub-divided by shape (tubular, barrel, goblet, hourglass, kettle, frame).
  • 22 Plucked drums: a string fixed to the skin is plucked, so the skin sounds: the Baul gopichand (ektara), the khamak and the Rajasthani bhapang.
  • 23 Friction drums: a stick or cord rubbed against the skin: the Brazilian cuíca, the Spanish zambomba.
  • 24 Singing membranes (kazoos): the voice makes a membrane buzz: the kazoo, the comb-and-paper.

  • 31 Simple chordophones (zithers): the strings run along a body that is just a string-bearer: santoor, qanun, koto, guzheng, the piano and harpsichord (board zithers with keyboards), the rudra veena and vichitra veena (stick zithers), the Malagasy valiha (tube zither).
  • 32 Composite chordophones: the string-bearer and resonator are joined and the resonator cannot be removed without destroying the instrument. Includes lutes (strings parallel to the body: sitar, sarod, Saraswati veena, guitar, violin, oud), harps (strings at right angles to the body) and harp-lutes (the kora).
  • How they are played: a suffix shows plucking, bowing, striking or a keyboard, so the violin and the guitar share a class (necked box lutes, 321.322) but differ in suffix.

  • 41 Free aerophones: the air vibrates but is not enclosed: the bullroarer, the whip; free reeds such as the harmonium, harmonica, accordion, sheng and khaen belong here (412.13).
  • 421 Edge-blown (flutes): air is split on an edge: end-blown (shakuhachi, ney), side-blown (bansuri, concert flute), duct or fipple flutes (recorder, algoza, tin whistle), vessel flutes (ocarina, xun) and panpipes.
  • 422 Reed aerophones: a reed chops the air: double reeds (shehnai, nadaswaram, oboe, bassoon, duduk), single reeds (clarinet, saxophone, the pungi), capped reeds (crumhorn) and bagpipes (mashak).
  • 423 Trumpets (lip-vibrated): the player's lips buzz: trumpet, trombone, tuba, horn, didgeridoo, shankh, karnal, ransingha.

  • Electro-acoustic: an acoustic vibration picked up and amplified: the electric guitar, the electric piano (Rhodes).
  • Electro-mechanical: a moving part makes an electric signal: the Hammond organ's tonewheels, the Telharmonium.
  • Electronic (analogue and digital): sound made by circuits or computers: theremin, synthesizers, drum machines, samplers, software instruments. The MIMO revision (2011) re-organised this class.

  • Example: the bansuri is 421.121.12 (a side-blown flute, open, with finger holes); the tabla's right-hand drum is a struck, single-headed, tubular membranophone with a tuning paste. You need not memorise numbers: the website shows them on each instrument page so museums and scholars can find a match.

sections.title: How the systems match (and a third from China)
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-03. The Indian and the European systems agree on four of five classes. The key difference: India sorts by the material in action, while Hornbostel–Sachs adds a second level by how the instrument is built. China's bayin (eight sounds), recorded in the Zhou dynasty texts, sorts by the material it is made of.

  • INS-03.1 Where they disagree: the harmonium is a sushira instrument in India but a "free aerophone" in H–S; the gopichand looks like a string instrument (tata) but H–S calls it a plucked drum because the skin, not the string, gives the tone. The piano is a struck zither (H–S), but many Indian writers treat it as a keyboard tata vadya.
  • INS-03.2 Classing by role, not sound: orchestras and bands sort by role: strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion, keyboards. This is why the flute (often metal) is a "woodwind" and the saxophone (brass) is also a woodwind (it uses a reed).
  • INS-03.3 Other systems: the Javanese gamelan groups instruments by musical function (melody, elaboration, punctuation); West African griot traditions group by caste and ceremony; the Indian Naubat or Naqqar khana courts grouped drums and shehnai as royal ensembles.
  • INS-03.4 Our choice: each instrument in this booklet carries both the Indian vadya and the H–S class, so Indian learners and world museums read the same map.

parts.title: The Families of Instruments
parts.intro: About this Part. Every family, with every main type. Each entry gives, in one or two lines: what it is, what it is made of, how it sounds, where it comes from and who made it famous. The tag after the name shows the Indian class (Tata, Sushira, Avanaddha, Ghana) and the Hornbostel–Sachs class (H–S). Families run from wind to strings to drums to solids to electronics, then DIY.

sections.title: Flutes: edge-blown aerophones
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-04. In a flute the player's breath is split on a sharp edge, and the air column inside vibrates. Fingers or keys change the column's length. Sushira · H–S 421. See also: MUS-01 (bansuri in Hindustani music), INS-00.01 (oldest flutes).

  • Bansuri (bansi, baanhi): North Indian bamboo flute with six or seven holes; Pannalal Ghosh (1911–1960) made a longer bass bansuri fit for classical music; Hariprasad Chaurasia took it to the world; Rakesh Chaurasia, Ronu Majumdar, Pravin Godkhindi today.
  • Venu (pullanguzhal, Carnatic flute): South Indian bamboo flute, usually eight holes; the instrument of Krishna in temple art; T. R. Mahalingam ("Mali") remade its style in the 1930s–40s; N. Ramani, Shashank Subramanyam.
  • Murali: a name for Krishna's flute in poetry; in practice the bansuri or venu.
  • Western concert flute: silver, gold or nickel; the modern key system was designed by Theobald Boehm (cylindrical flute, 1847); Jean-Pierre Rampal, James Galway, Emmanuel Pahud.
  • Piccolo: half-size concert flute, an octave higher; the brightest voice in the orchestra and marching band.
  • Dizi (China): bamboo flute with an extra hole covered by a thin reed membrane (dimo) that gives a buzzing brightness.
  • Fife: small high flute of military bands and folk music (Europe, Americas).
  • Irish wooden flute: simple-system flute of Irish traditional music; Matt Molloy.
  • Ryuteki and shinobue (Japan): transverse bamboo flutes of gagaku court music and festivals.

  • Shakuhachi (Japan): bamboo, five holes, blown across a sharp edge at the top; played by Zen komuso monks as meditation (suizen).
  • Ney (Persia, Turkey, the Arab world): reed flute of Sufi music; Rumi's Masnavi opens with "Listen to the ney".
  • Quena (Andes): notched bamboo or bone flute of Peru and Bolivia; heard in "El Cóndor Pasa".
  • Kaval (Balkans): long, end-blown shepherd's flute.
  • Native American (Plains) flute: technically a duct flute with an external block; revived by R. Carlos Nakai.

  • Recorder: wooden or plastic duct flute, a family from sopranino to great bass; Renaissance and Baroque music; the classroom instrument of millions.
  • Tin whistle (penny whistle): cheap metal duct flute of Irish and Scottish music.
  • Algoza (alghoza, satara, jodiya pava): a pair of duct flutes played together, one as drone; Rajasthan, Punjab, Sindh, Kutch.
  • Flageolet and gemshorn: historical European duct flutes.
  • Bamboo flutes of Adivasi India: many tribal communities of central and eastern India have their own bamboo flutes, often played by herders; each will get a page once verified with local sources.

  • Ocarina: clay or plastic egg-shaped flute; modern form by Giuseppe Donati of Budrio, Italy (1853); famous again through video games.
  • Xun (China): one of the oldest Chinese instruments, clay egg with finger holes; examples about 7,000 years old.
  • Gemshorn and clay whistles: animal horn or clay bird-whistles of many cultures; clay whistles from the Indus civilisation.

  • Siku / zampoña (Andes): played in pairs that interlock notes; nai (Romania), made world-famous by Gheorghe Zamfir; syrinx (ancient Greece, the pipes of Pan); paixiao (China).

  • Nose flutes of Hawaii (ʻohe hano ihu), the Philippines, Borneo, Taiwan and Polynesia: breath from the nose, thought to be purer than breath from the mouth.

  • Pungi (been) is not a flute: the snake-charmer's pungi blows into a gourd that feeds two cane pipes, each with a single beating reed. It is a reed aerophone (double clarinet, H–S 422.22), listed in INS-05. (The snake does not hear the tune; it follows the movement of the pungi.)

sections.title: Reed instruments: reed aerophones and free reeds
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-05. A reed is a thin strip (cane, palm leaf, metal or plastic) that opens and shuts many times a second, chopping the air. In a double reed two blades beat against each other; in a single reed one blade beats against a mouthpiece; in a free reed a metal tongue swings through a slot. Sushira · H–S 422 and 412.13.

  • Shehnai: North Indian double-reed of weddings and temples, wooden tube with metal bell; Ustad Bismillah Khan (1916–2006, Bharat Ratna 2001) brought it to the concert stage and played at the Red Fort on 15 August 1947.
  • Nadaswaram (nagaswaram): long South Indian double-reed, the most important temple instrument of Tamil Nadu, played with the thavil drum; T. N. Rajarathinam Pillai, Sheik Chinna Moulana.
  • Sundari: small shehnai of Maharashtra (Solapur).
  • Kuzhal (Kerala): short double-reed of temple ensembles.
  • Oboe, cor anglais, bassoon, contrabassoon: the Western double reeds; the oboe gives the orchestra's tuning A.
  • Duduk (Armenia): apricot-wood double reed with a very wide reed; dark and mournful; UNESCO lists it as Intangible Cultural Heritage (2005/2008); Djivan Gasparyan.
  • Zurna, surnay, suona, sorna: loud outdoor double reeds of Turkey, Persia, Central Asia and China, family cousins of the shehnai.
  • Hichiriki (Japan) and piri (Korea): short bamboo double reeds of court music.

  • Clarinet: wooden single-reed developed by Johann Christoph Denner in Nuremberg around 1700; behaves like a closed tube (strong odd harmonics); Benny Goodman, Sabine Meyer. In India, A. K. C. Natarajan played Carnatic clarinet.
  • Saxophone: brass body, single reed; patented by Adolphe Sax in 1846; the voice of jazz; Kadri Gopalnath (1949–2019) made it a Carnatic instrument.
  • Pungi / been: gourd-and-reed double clarinet of snake charmers and the Kalbeliya of Rajasthan; the "been" sound in film songs is often a keyboard copy.
  • Launeddas (Sardinia): triple clarinet of cane, played with circular breathing.
  • Arghul (Egypt), mijwiz (Levant): double clarinets.

  • Mashak (mashakbeen): bagpipe of Rajasthan, Uttarakhand and Himachal; goatskin bag; played at weddings and in the Kumaon chholiya dance.
  • Great Highland bagpipe (Scotland), uilleann pipes (Ireland, bellows-blown, quiet and sweet), gaita (Galicia, Asturias), zampogna (Italy), musette (France), tulum (Turkey).

  • Sheng (China): mouth organ of bamboo pipes in a cup, each with a metal free reed; over 3,000 years old; the ancestor of the harmonica and accordion idea.
  • Khaen (Laos, north-east Thailand): bamboo free-reed mouth organ; UNESCO 2017.
  • Shō (Japan): court mouth organ, a cousin of the sheng.
  • Harmonium: free-reed keyboard pumped by bellows; patented in France by Alexandre Debain (1840); the hand-pumped, floor-played version was made in Calcutta by Dwarkanath Ghose (Dwarkin & Son, 1875). Banned on All India Radio from 1940 to 1971 as "foreign" and "out of tune" with Indian microtones; now central to qawwali, bhajan, Sikh kirtan and natya sangeet.
  • Shruti box: a harmonium without keys, giving a drone.
  • Harmonica (mouth organ): small free-reed instrument, made popular by Matthias Hohner (Germany) from 1857; blues, folk; R. D. Burman's film songs used it.
  • Accordion: patented in Vienna by Cyrill Demian (1829); Bombay film orchestras used it widely (Kersi Lord was among its best-known players).
  • Bandoneón: square concertina from Germany (named after Heinrich Band) that became the soul of Argentine tango; Astor Piazzolla.
  • Concertina (England, Germany) and melodica (a keyboard you blow).

sections.title: Brass and lip-vibrated instruments
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-06. The player's lips buzz into a cup or opening, and the tube's air column picks the note. Valves or a slide add tube length. They need not be made of brass: the didgeridoo is wood and the shankh is shell. Sushira · H–S 423.

  • Shankh (conch): shell trumpet blown in Hindu and Buddhist rituals and in battle in the Mahabharata (Krishna's Panchajanya).
  • Karnal, ransingha (narsingha), turhi, bhongal, nagphani: long and curved brass horns of the Himalayan states, Rajasthan, Gujarat and Maharashtra; ritual, wedding and war signals.
  • Kombu (Kerala): curved horn of the panchavadyam temple ensemble.
  • Dungchen (Tibet): copper long horns of monasteries, up to three metres.
  • Shofar (Jewish ritual): ram's horn, sounded on Rosh Hashanah.
  • Didgeridoo (yidaki, Aboriginal Australia): eucalyptus trunk hollowed by termites; played with circular breathing for a continuous drone; at least 1,000 years old (rock art).
  • Alphorn (Swiss Alps), vuvuzela (South Africa), lur (Bronze Age Scandinavia), carnyx (Iron Age Celts), cornu (ancient Rome).

  • Trumpet: the high brass; valves invented by Heinrich Stölzel and Friedrich Blühmel (1810s); Louis Armstrong, Miles Davis, Wynton Marsalis; Indian film brass bands; Chic Chocolate in 1950s Bombay.
  • Cornet, flugelhorn, bugle: cousins with a softer or simpler sound; the bugle calls of armies.
  • French horn: coiled horn with a wide bell; hand in the bell; the warmest brass.
  • Trombone: a sliding tube; the only brass that glides between notes easily; Jack Teagarden, Christian Lindberg.
  • Tuba, euphonium, sousaphone: low brass; the tuba was patented by Wilhelm Wieprecht and Carl Moritz (Berlin, 1835); the sousaphone wraps around a marching player.
  • Saxhorns (Adolphe Sax's brass family), ophicleide and serpent (older bass instruments).
  • Indian wedding bands: the brass band (baaja) with trumpets, clarinets and drums, from British military bands, now a lively Indian tradition of its own.

sections.title: Plucked lutes
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-07. A lute has a neck along which the strings run parallel to a resonating body; the player shortens the strings by pressing them, with or without frets. Plucked with the fingers, nails or a plectrum (mizrab, pick). Tata · H–S 321.3. See also: INS-00.05 (jawari), MUS-01.

  • Sitar: long-necked lute with a gourd body, movable curved frets, 6–7 main and 11–13 sympathetic strings, and a jawari bridge; developed in its present form in 18th-century North India (the old story crediting Amir Khusrau is not supported by evidence); Ravi Shankar, Vilayat Khan, Nikhil Banerjee, Anoushka Shankar, Shahid Parvez.
  • Surbahar: bass sitar for slow, deep alap; Annapurna Devi, Imrat Khan.
  • Sarod: fretless lute with a skin belly and a polished steel fingerboard, plucked with a coconut-shell plectrum; descended from the Afghan rabab; Allauddin Khan, Ali Akbar Khan, Amjad Ali Khan, Buddhadev Das Gupta.
  • Saraswati veena: the great Carnatic lute of jackfruit wood with 24 fixed frets, four playing and three drone strings; held across the lap; Veena Dhanammal, S. Balachander, E. Gayathri, Jayanthi Kumaresh. Thanjavur and Bobbili (Andhra Pradesh) veenas carry Geographical Indication tags.
  • Chitra veena (gottuvadyam): fretless Carnatic lute played with a slide; Narayan Iyengar, N. Ravikiran.
  • Tanpura (tambura): four- to six-string drone lute, never melodic; the "sound carpet" behind all Indian classical music; Miraj (Maharashtra) sitars and tanpuras received a GI tag in 2024.
  • Rudra veena (been) is a stick zither, see INS-09; mohan veena is a modified slide guitar (INS-07.3).
  • Rabab (rubab): short-necked, skin-bellied lute of Afghanistan, Kashmir and Punjab; Bhai Mardana played the rabab for Guru Nanak.
  • Dotara (dotar): two- or four-string folk lute of Bengal and Assam, of the Baul and Bhawaiya singers.
  • Tumbi: single-string Punjabi lute with a high, bright twang; Lal Chand Yamla Jatt.
  • Sursingar, swarbat, kachapi veena: rarer historical lutes of North and South India, now mostly in museums.

  • Oud (ud): short-necked, fretless, pear-shaped lute of the Arab world, Turkey and Persia; the word gave Europe "lute" (al-ud); Munir Bashir, Anouar Brahem.
  • Saz / bağlama (Turkey), tar and setar (Iran, Azerbaijan), tanbur (Kurdish and Persian), dutar (Central Asia), dombra (Kazakhstan, the national instrument), komuz (Kyrgyzstan).
  • Pipa (China): pear-shaped lute played upright, with rapid tremolo; Wu Man. Biwa (Japan) is its relative, used for epic tales.
  • Shamisen (Japan): three-string, long-necked, skin-covered lute plucked with a large plectrum; kabuki and folk (Tsugaru-jamisen). Its ancestor is the Chinese sanxian.
  • Ngoni (West Africa): small lute of the griots, possible ancestor of the banjo; Bassekou Kouyaté. Gimbri / guembri (Morocco): bass lute of Gnawa trance music.

  • Lute (European): Renaissance favourite, with a bowl back; John Dowland's songs.
  • Classical guitar: Spanish six-string; the modern body was set by Antonio de Torres (1850s–1880s); Andrés Segovia made it a concert instrument; Julian Bream, John Williams.
  • Flamenco guitar: lighter, brighter; Paco de Lucía.
  • Steel-string acoustic guitar: C. F. Martin & Co. (founded 1833 in New York, later Nazareth, Pennsylvania); folk, country, Bollywood strumming.
  • Slide and resonator guitars: Hawaiian (lap) steel guitar, Dobro; in India, Brij Bhushan Kabra (Hindustani slide guitar) and Vishwa Mohan Bhatt (mohan veena; Grammy 1994 with Ry Cooder for A Meeting by the River).
  • Mandolin: Italian, four double courses tuned like a violin; U. Srinivas ("Mandolin Srinivas", 1969–2014) made it a Carnatic instrument; bluegrass (Bill Monroe).
  • Banjo: skin-headed lute from African ancestors (the akonting and others) brought by enslaved people to the Americas; bluegrass (Earl Scruggs), Béla Fleck. In India the "banjo" is the Japanese taishōgoto keyed zither (see INS-09).
  • Ukulele: small four-string lute made in Hawaii from the Portuguese machete brought by Madeiran immigrants in 1879; easy first instrument.
  • Balalaika (Russia, triangular), bouzouki (Greece), Portuguese guitar (fado), charango (Andes; small, ten strings, once made of armadillo shell), cuatro (Venezuela, Puerto Rico), tres (Cuba), vihuela and guitarrón (Mexican mariachi), cavaquinho (Portugal, Brazil).
  • Bass guitar and double bass: see INS-08 (bowed) and INS-13 (electric).

sections.title: Bowed strings
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-08. A bow of horsehair coated with rosin grips and releases the string hundreds of times a second (a "stick-slip" motion), so the note can last and swell. Bowed instruments probably began in Central Asia around the 9th–10th century. Tata · H–S 321 or 31 with bowed suffix (-71).

  • Sarangi: carved from a single block of wood (often tun), covered with goatskin, played with the fingernails pressing the strings from the side; about 35–40 sympathetic strings; the closest instrument to the human voice; Pandit Ram Narayan (1927–2024) made it a solo concert instrument; Sultan Khan, Kamal Sabri. Folk sarangis: the Sindhi sindhi sarangi, gujratan and jogiya sarangis of Rajasthan.
  • Kamaicha: bowed lute of the Manganiyar community of western Rajasthan, with a large round skin-covered belly and deep, booming tone.
  • Ravanhatha: one of the oldest bowed instruments of India; bamboo neck, coconut-shell body; played by the Bhopa singers of Rajasthan and Gujarat telling the tale of Pabuji; named in legend after Ravana.
  • Esraj and dilruba: fretted bowed instruments with sympathetic strings; esraj in Bengal (Rabindra Sangeet, Santiniketan), dilruba in Punjab and Sikh kirtan; the taus (peacock-shaped) is said to have been designed for Guru Hargobind.
  • Violin in India: adopted into Carnatic music around 1800, credited to Baluswami Dikshitar; played sitting, scroll resting on the foot; Lalgudi Jayaraman, M. S. Gopalakrishnan, L. Subramaniam, Kanyakumari; in Hindustani music N. Rajam and V. G. Jog.
  • Pena (Manipur): coconut-shell bowed lute with a bamboo neck, played by Meitei bards.
  • Banam (Santal and other Adivasi communities), chikara (Rajasthan, Uttarakhand), sarinda (Bengal, Assam, Punjab): folk fiddles.

  • Violin: four strings, no frets; the oldest surviving violins come from Andrea Amati in Cremona (1550s–60s); peak of craft with Antonio Stradivari (c. 1644–1737) and Giuseppe Guarneri "del Gesù" (1698–1744); Paganini, Heifetz, Menuhin, Perlman, Mutter, Hilary Hahn.
  • Viola: larger, a fifth lower, a darker voice.
  • Cello: played between the knees; Pablo Casals (Bach suites), Jacqueline du Pré, Mstislav Rostropovich, Yo-Yo Ma.
  • Double bass: lowest bowed string (from the viol family in shape); jazz plucks it (Charles Mingus, Ray Brown).
  • Viols (viola da gamba): fretted, older family played resting on the leg; revived by Jordi Savall.
  • Hardanger fiddle (Norway, with sympathetic strings), nyckelharpa (Sweden, keyed fiddle), gusle (Balkans, epic singing), rebec and vielle (medieval), hurdy-gurdy (a wheel bows the strings, turned by a crank).

  • Erhu (China): two strings with the bow trapped between them; snake-skin resonator; Abing's Erquan Yingyue (Moon Reflected on the Second Spring).
  • Morin khuur (Mongolia): horse-head fiddle; UNESCO Intangible Heritage (2003/2008); its legend tells of a horse turned into music.
  • Kamancheh (Iran, Azerbaijan), kemençe (Turkey, Greece), rebab (Arab world, Java, Malaysia; ancestor of many fiddles), haegeum (Korea), kokyū (Japan), sarinda (Afghanistan).
  • Masenqo (Ethiopia; one-string fiddle of the azmari singers), imzad (one-string fiddle played by Tuareg women; UNESCO 2013), goje (West Africa).

sections.title: Zithers, harps and lyres
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-09. In a zither the strings run across a board, box, tube or stick with no neck; in a harp they rise from the body at an angle; in a lyre they run from the body to a crossbar. Tata · H–S 31 (zithers), 322 (harps), 321.2 (lyres).

  • Santoor: hammered trapezoid zither of Kashmir with about 100 strings in groups; once used in Sufiana music; Pandit Shivkumar Sharma (1938–2022) made it a classical solo instrument; Bhajan Sopori, Rahul Sharma.
  • Rudra veena (been): stick zither with two large gourds and raised frets; the most sacred instrument of Hindustani music and the dhrupad style; Asad Ali Khan, Zia Mohiuddin Dagar, Bahauddin Dagar.
  • Vichitra veena: fretless stick zither played with a glass slide; Lalmani Misra, Gopal Krishna.
  • Swarmandal: plucked board zither used by singers for a shimmering backdrop (Bade Ghulam Ali Khan).
  • Bulbul tarang (Indian banjo): a keyed zither from the Japanese taishōgoto, popular in folk and qawwali; in Pakistan's Balochistan called benju.
  • Yazh: ancient Tamil harp or lyre praised in Sangam literature; now lost, with modern reconstructions.
  • Kinnari, gettuvadyam and onavillu: folk stick zithers and musical bows of the south (the kinnari of Telangana bards; the onavillu is struck during Onam at the Padmanabhaswamy temple, Kerala).

  • Guqin (China): seven-string fretless zither, the instrument of scholars and Confucius; about 3,000 years old; UNESCO 2003/2008.
  • Guzheng (China), koto (Japan, 13 strings; Michio Miyagi), gayageum (Korea, 12 strings; Hwang Byungki), đàn tranh (Vietnam): the plucked long zither family with movable bridges.
  • Đàn bầu (Vietnam): one-string zither played by bending a flexible rod, giving gliding notes.
  • Qanun (Arab world, Turkey): trapezoid plucked zither with small levers for microtones.
  • Santur (Iran), yangqin (China), cimbalom (Hungary; Kodály, Liszt), hammered dulcimer (Britain, the Americas): the hammered zither family, cousins of the santoor.
  • Kantele (Finland; the Kalevala's magic instrument), kanklės (Lithuania), gusli (Russia), psaltery (medieval).
  • Concert zither (Alpine), autoharp (USA folk), Appalachian dulcimer (fretted, played on the lap).
  • Valiha (Madagascar): bamboo tube zither, strings cut from the bamboo skin or made of wire; national instrument.

  • Lyres and harps of Ur (Iraq): found by Leonard Woolley in the Royal Cemetery about 1927–29, dated around 2500 BCE; the "Bull-headed Lyre" is among the oldest stringed instruments.
  • Ancient Indian vina (arched harp): the early "vina" was a bow-shaped harp, shown in Bharhut, Sanchi and Amaravati sculptures and on the gold coins of Samudragupta (4th century CE), who is shown playing it.
  • Saung-gauk (Myanmar): boat-shaped arched harp, the national instrument, a living relative of the old Indian vina.
  • Concert pedal harp: 47 strings and seven pedals; the double-action pedal was patented by Sébastien Érard (1810).
  • Celtic harp (cláirseach): Irish wire-strung harp; the "Brian Boru" harp at Trinity College Dublin (around the 14th–15th century) is Ireland's national symbol; Turlough O'Carolan.
  • Paraguayan and Andean harps, Welsh triple harp, angle harps of ancient Egypt and Persia (chang).
  • Kora (West Africa): 21-string harp-lute of the Mandinka griots, with a calabash body; Toumani Diabaté (1965–2024); Sona Jobarteh.

  • Kithara and lyra (ancient Greece): Apollo's instrument; the word "lyric" comes from it.
  • Krar and begena (Ethiopia): bowl lyre and large box lyre for prayer.
  • Obokano (Kenya), simsimiyya (Egypt, Yemen), Anglo-Saxon lyre (Sutton Hoo, 7th century).

sections.title: Keyboard instruments
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-10. A keyboard is a control system, not a sound source: keys can open organ pipes, pluck or strike strings, or switch circuits. So keyboards cross the classes: the organ is an aerophone, the piano a struck zither, the harmonium a free reed and the synthesizer an electrophone.
  • INS-10.1 Hydraulis: water organ invented by Ctesibius of Alexandria (3rd century BCE); the first keyboard instrument.
  • INS-10.2 Pipe organ: pipes blown by bellows, played from keyboards and pedals; church and cathedral music; J. S. Bach. UNESCO lists German organ craft and music (2017).
  • INS-10.3 Clavichord: strings struck by small brass blades; quiet, expressive; favourite for home practice in the 18th century.
  • INS-10.4 Harpsichord: strings plucked by quills; Baroque music; Domenico Scarlatti, François Couperin; Wanda Landowska revived it in the 20th century.
  • INS-10.5 Piano: invented by Bartolomeo Cristofori in Florence around 1700 as the gravicembalo col piano e forte (harpsichord with soft and loud); three Cristofori pianos survive, the oldest (1720) at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. The cast-iron frame (1820s–40s), cross-stringing and Steinway & Sons (New York, 1853) made the modern grand. Upright, baby grand, concert grand (88 keys since about 1880).
  • INS-10.6 Celesta: hammers strike steel plates; patented by Auguste Mustel (1886); the "Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy" (Tchaikovsky, 1892).
  • INS-10.7 Harmonium, accordion, melodica: free-reed keyboards (see INS-05.4).
  • INS-10.8 Electric and electronic keyboards: Hammond organ (1935), Fender Rhodes electric piano, Wurlitzer, Hohner Clavinet, Mellotron (tape playback, 1960s), synthesizers, digital pianos, and the home keyboards (Casio, Yamaha) that taught a generation in India. See INS-13.
  • INS-10.9 Keyboards in Indian music: harmonium; the piano in Calcutta and Bombay homes and church music; A. R. Rahman and other composers working from keyboards and synths; the swarmandal-like use of synth pads.

sections.title: Drums: membranophones
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-11. A drum is a skin (or plastic) stretched over a shell or frame. Most drums give unclear, "inharmonic" overtones, so they are felt as rhythm rather than melody. India's loaded-skin drums (tabla, mridangam, pakhawaj) are the great exception (INS-00.03). Avanaddha · H–S 2. See also: MUS-12 (tala), INS-02.2.

  • Tabla: pair of drums, the wooden dayan (right) and the metal or clay bayan (left), each with a black syahi; the main drum of Hindustani music since the 18th century; gharanas of Delhi, Ajrara, Lucknow, Farukhabad, Benares and Punjab; Ahmed Jan Thirakwa, Alla Rakha, Kishan Maharaj, Zakir Hussain (1951–2024), Anindo Chatterjee, Swapan Chaudhuri, Anuradha Pal.
  • Pakhawaj: barrel drum with two heads, ancestor-cousin of the tabla; accompanies dhrupad and temple music; Kudau Singh, Raja Chhatrapati Singh, Pandit Bhavani Shankar.
  • Mridangam: Carnatic double-headed barrel drum of jackfruit wood, the right head with a permanent black paste, the left with a wet wheat paste applied before playing; Palghat Mani Iyer, Umayalpuram Sivaraman, Karaikudi Mani, Trichy Sankaran.
  • Thavil: barrel drum played with a stick and capped fingers alongside the nadaswaram; Valayapatti Subramaniam.
  • Kanjira: small frame drum with one pair of jingles; once covered with monitor-lizard skin (now banned under the Wildlife Protection Act, so goatskin is used); G. Harishankar, V. Selvaganesh.
  • Mardala (Odisha, Odissi music), khol (clay drum of Bengal, Assam and Odisha kirtan), pung (Manipur; the pung cholom drum dance), mizhavu (large copper pot drum of Kerala's Koodiyattam).

  • Dhol: big double-headed barrel drum played with sticks; Punjab bhangra, Gujarat garba, Assam Bihu, the dhol-tasha processions of Pune.
  • Dholak: smaller two-headed hand drum of weddings, qawwali and film songs.
  • Nagara (naqqara): pair of kettle drums of Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and the royal naubat ensembles; played at temples and the dargah of Ajmer.
  • Chenda (Kerala): cylindrical drum played with sticks; the thundering chenda melam of temple festivals and Kathakali; Peruvanam Kuttan Marar.
  • Edakka (idakka): Kerala hourglass drum whose pitch changes as the player squeezes its strings: it can play melodies.
  • Maddalam and timila: barrel and hourglass drums of Kerala's panchavadyam (five instruments: timila, maddalam, ilathalam, idakka and kombu).
  • Damaru: small two-headed hourglass drum rattled by beads on strings; Shiva's drum; the fourteen Maheshwara Sutras of Sanskrit grammar are said, in legend, to have sounded from it.
  • Hudka (hurka): hourglass drum of Uttarakhand and Himachal bards.
  • Dhak (Bengal): large drum of Durga Puja, played with sticks and hung from the shoulder.
  • Chang (daf): frame drum of Rajasthan's Holi songs and Punjab; halgi of Maharashtra; tasha (kettle drum played with sticks).
  • Parai (thappu): Tamil frame drum, long linked to caste oppression and now reclaimed as a proud art of Dalit cultural movements.
  • Urumi (Tamil Nadu, hourglass with a friction-like groan), dollu (Karnataka; Dollu Kunitha dance), dappu (Telangana and Andhra), mandar (Jharkhand), nagada and tamak (Adivasi drums of central India), madal (Nepal and the hills), ghumot (Goa's clay pot drum, declared Goa's heritage instrument in 2019).

  • Djembe (West Africa, Mali and Guinea): goblet drum of the Mandinka, carved from one log; bass, tone and slap strokes; Mamady Keïta.
  • Talking drum (dùndún) (Yoruba, Nigeria): hourglass drum squeezed under the arm to copy the tones of speech.
  • Darbuka (doumbek, tabla in Arabic): goblet drum of the Middle East and North Africa.
  • Daf, bendir, riq, tar: frame drums of Persia, North Africa and the Arab world; bodhrán (Ireland); tambourine (Europe); pandeiro (Brazil).
  • Taiko (Japan): big barrel drums; kumi-daiko ensemble style since the 1950s (Daihachi Oguchi); Kodo.
  • Janggu (Korea): hourglass drum of court and folk music.
  • Conga, bongo and timbales (Cuba): Afro-Cuban drums of salsa and Latin jazz; Mongo Santamaría, Tito Puente.
  • Surdo, repinique, caixa (Brazil): samba school drums; atabaque for candomblé and capoeira.
  • Timpani (kettle drums): tuned copper bowls with pedals; the orchestra's thunder.
  • Snare drum and bass drum: military origins; the snare's wires give a crisp rattle.
  • Drum kit (drum set): one player with bass drum, snare, toms, hi-hat and cymbals; grew in New Orleans and vaudeville; the bass-drum pedal patented by William F. Ludwig (1909); Gene Krupa, Buddy Rich, Max Roach, John Bonham; in India Sivamani, Ranjit Barot.
  • Frame and hand drums of the Americas: the Native American powwow drum, Hawaiian pahu, Peruvian bombo.
  • Plucked and friction drums: the Baul gopichand (ektara), khamak and Rajasthan's bhapang (plucked drums, INS-02.2); the Brazilian cuíca (friction drum, the "laughing" sound of samba).

sections.title: Idiophones: gongs, bells, cymbals, xylophones and lamellophones
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-12. In an idiophone the whole solid body vibrates: metal, wood, stone, clay, glass or bamboo. They include the oldest and the newest instruments (stone chimes and the handpan). Ghana · H–S 1.

  • Ghatam: clay pot of the Carnatic ensemble, played with fingers, palms and the stomach pressing the mouth; the best are made at Manamadurai (Tamil Nadu); T. H. "Vikku" Vinayakram (Grammy 1992, Planet Drum), Suresh Vaidyanathan.
  • Morsing (morchang): jaw harp of Carnatic music (morsing) and Rajasthani folk (morchang).
  • Manjira, jhanj, kartal, tala, elathalam: hand cymbals of bhajan, kirtan and temple music; gini (Odisha) and the large cymbals of Manipuri cymbal cholom.
  • Khartal (kartal): pairs of wooden clappers of the Manganiyar and Langa musicians of Rajasthan, played in dazzling rhythms.
  • Chimta: long fire-tongs with jingles; Punjabi folk and Sikh kirtan.
  • Jal tarang: porcelain bowls filled with water to different levels and struck with sticks; Milind Tulankar.
  • Ghungroo: ankle bells of Kathak and folk dancers.
  • Ghanta: temple bells; bell metal (kansa) bells of Odisha and Bengal.
  • Musical pillars: carved stone pillars that ring at different pitches, at the Vittala temple in Hampi, Nellaiappar temple in Tirunelveli and others.
  • Thali, kansya and kaasi: bell-metal plates struck in folk music; the gogona (Assam's bamboo jaw harp of Bihu) and toka (split-bamboo clapper).

  • Gamelan (Indonesia: Java and Bali): orchestras of bronze gongs (gong ageng), kettle-gongs (bonang), metallophones (saron, gender) and drums; UNESCO 2021; inspired Debussy after the Paris Exposition of 1889.
  • Kulintang (southern Philippines, Borneo), khong wong (Thailand), gong cultural space of the Central Highlands (Vietnam, UNESCO 2005/2008).
  • Bianzhong (China): the set of 65 bronze bells from the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng (433 BCE); each bell gives two different notes depending on where it is struck.
  • Church and carillon bells (Europe), temple bells (Japan's bonshō), singing bowls (Himalayas), cowbells (Swiss, Latin).
  • Cymbals: the Zildjian company was founded in Constantinople in 1623 and now works in Massachusetts; crash, ride, hi-hat, China cymbals.
  • Triangle, tubular bells, crotales: orchestral metal idiophones.

  • Balafon (West Africa): wooden-keyed xylophone with gourd resonators; the Sosso Bala, kept in Guinea since the 13th century, is in UNESCO's first list (2001/2008).
  • Marimba: resonated xylophone of African origin, national instrument of Guatemala; concert marimba; the timbila of the Chopi of Mozambique (UNESCO 2005/2008).
  • Xylophone, glockenspiel, vibraphone (vibraphone with motor-driven vibrato, 1920s; Lionel Hampton, Gary Burton).
  • Ranat ek (Thailand), gambang (Indonesia), amadinda (Uganda).
  • Steelpan (steel drum): tuned from oil drums in Trinidad and Tobago in the 1930s–40s; national instrument; Ellie Mannette, Winston "Spree" Simon; steel orchestras at Carnival.

  • Mbira (Zimbabwe, Shona): metal tongues on a wooden board, often inside a gourd with rattles; sacred bira ceremonies; UNESCO 2020 (Malawi and Zimbabwe). Relatives: sanza, likembe, kalimba (commercial version made popular by Hugh Tracey, 1950s–60s).
  • Jaw harp: metal or bamboo tongue plucked in front of the mouth, which shapes the overtones; found in Rajasthan (morchang), Assam (gogona), Siberia (khomus), Austria (Maultrommel).
  • Music box: a pinned cylinder plucks steel teeth; Switzerland, 18th century.

  • Rattles: maracas, shekere (gourd with beads), rain stick, ankle rattles; angklung (Sundanese bamboo tubes shaken in a frame, UNESCO 2010).
  • Scrapers and clappers: güiro, washboard, claves, castanets (Spain), spoons, wood block, slapstick, the cajón (Afro-Peruvian box drum, sat on and slapped; Peru's national heritage since 2001).
  • Udu (Nigeria): clay pot with a side hole, struck and cupped for a bass "bloop".
  • Friction idiophones: the glass harmonica (Benjamin Franklin, 1761; Mozart wrote for it), the musical saw, rubbed singing bowls.
  • Handpan (Hang): steel sound sculpture invented by Felix Rohner and Sabina Schärer of PANArt, Bern (2000); hundreds of makers now build similar "handpans".
  • Tongue drum (steel tongue drum), waterphone, Array mbira: new 20th–21st century idiophones.

sections.title: Electronic and electric instruments: electrophones
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-13. Electrophones turn electricity into sound or amplify a vibration electrically (INS-00.06). They became the fifth class in 1940. See also: TEC (audio and computing), MUS-15 (technology and listening).

  • Telharmonium: Thaddeus Cahill's 200-tonne machine (1897 patent; demonstrated 1906) sent music down telephone lines.
  • Theremin: Leon Theremin (Lev Termen), around 1920; played without touch; Clara Rockmore; the eerie sound of 1950s science-fiction films.
  • Ondes Martenot: Maurice Martenot (1928); a ring on a wire controls pitch; Messiaen's Turangalîla-Symphonie, film scores; Jonny Greenwood.
  • Trautonium (1930): used for the bird sounds of Hitchcock's The Birds (1963).
  • Hammond organ: Laurens Hammond (1935); spinning tonewheels; with the Leslie rotating speaker, the voice of gospel, jazz and rock (Jimmy Smith).

  • Rickenbacker "Frying Pan" (George Beauchamp and Adolph Rickenbacker, 1931–32): early electric lap steel guitar.
  • Solid-body guitars: Les Paul's "Log" (about 1941); the Fender Telecaster (sold from 1950–51 as the Broadcaster, then Telecaster), the Gibson Les Paul (1952), the Fender Stratocaster (1954); Chuck Berry, Jimi Hendrix, Eric Clapton, Jimmy Page, Prince.
  • Electric bass: the Fender Precision Bass (1951); James Jamerson, Jaco Pastorius.
  • Amplifiers and effects: valve amps (Marshall, Vox, Fender), distortion, wah, delay, looper pedals.
  • Electric guitar in India: 1960s Calcutta and Bombay bands; film-song guitar; Indian rock (Indian Ocean, Parikrama); Carnatic electric guitar (Prasanna).

  • Moog modular (Robert Moog, 1964) and Minimoog (1970): voltage-controlled oscillators, filters and envelopes; Wendy Carlos, Switched-On Bach (1968).
  • Buchla (Don Buchla, West Coast), ARP, EMS VCS3, Prophet-5 (polyphonic, with memory, 1978).
  • Yamaha DX7 (1983): affordable digital FM synthesis, based on John Chowning's research at Stanford; the sound of 1980s pop, including Indian film music.
  • Roland, Korg, Casio: Japanese makers who put synths in every school and home; Ikutaro Kakehashi founded Roland (1972).
  • Synth artists: Kraftwerk, Vangelis, Jean-Michel Jarre, Isao Tomita, Giorgio Moroder; in India, Charanjit Singh's Synthesizing: Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat (1982), an early acid-house sound years before Chicago's.

  • Drum machines: Wurlitzer Sideman (1959); Roland TR-808 (1980) and TR-909 (1983), the beats of hip-hop and house; Linn LM-1.
  • Samplers: Mellotron (tape, 1960s), Fairlight CMI (1979), E-mu Emulator, Akai MPC (1988), the hip-hop producer's instrument.
  • MIDI (1983): a shared language that lets keyboards, drum pads and computers control each other.
  • Pads and controllers: the Roland Octapad (from 1985), central to Bollywood and Indian devotional music; Ableton Push, Launchpad; the ROLI Seaboard (2013) and other expressive controllers.
  • Indian electronic instruments: the electronic tanpura and tala (tabla) machines (Radel, Raagini and others), Riyaz apps, and the digital shruti box.

  • Software instruments: DAWs (Ableton Live, FL Studio, Logic), virtual instruments and sample libraries of Indian instruments.
  • Auto-Tune (Andy Hildebrand, Antares, 1997): pitch correction that became an effect (Cher's "Believe", 1998; T-Pain).
  • AI instruments: neural synthesis such as Google Magenta's NSynth (2017); voice-to-instrument models; the questions they raise are discussed in MUS-00.08 and INS-29.
  • Live coding and laptop orchestras: music made by writing code on stage (Sonic Pi, TidalCycles).

sections.title: DIY, found and recycled instruments
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-14. Anyone can build an instrument from what is at home. Making one is the best way to understand the physics in Part 7. See also: INS-26, SNT (physics of sound in the Curriculum Index).
  • INS-14.1 Water-glass xylophone: glasses with different water levels; less water, higher note (a home jal tarang).
  • INS-14.2 Straw oboe and paper kazoo: flatten and cut a straw to make a double reed; hum through comb and paper.
  • INS-14.3 Rubber-band and shoebox guitars, cigar-box guitars: show length and tension (Mersenne's laws); the cigar-box guitar has a long history in American blues.
  • INS-14.4 PVC and bamboo flutes: drill holes in a pipe; tune by enlarging.
  • INS-14.5 Washtub bass, jug and washboard: the jug bands of the American South; skiffle in 1950s Britain.
  • INS-14.6 Bucket drumming, pots and pans: street drumming; Indian folk musicians' use of the matka (water pot) and the steel thali.
  • INS-14.7 Recycled orchestras: the Recycled Orchestra of Cateura (Paraguay), whose violins and cellos are made from landfill waste; the stage show Stomp (1991).
  • INS-14.8 Makerspace electronics: Arduino synths, the Stylophone, contact microphones, circuit bending of toys.
  • INS-14.9 Safety and care: sand sharp edges, use food-safe materials for mouthpieces, and keep volume safe for ears (MUS-22).

parts.title: The World Map of Instruments
parts.intro: About this Part. The same instruments, now arranged by place: India state by state in depth, then each continent. Families are in Part 2; this Part answers "what do people play here?" The Instrument Register at the end (INS-19.4) gives the full record fields for 30 landmark instruments.

sections.title: India, state by state
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-15. India may have more living instrument traditions than any other country. Many belong to hereditary musician communities (Manganiyar, Langa, Bhopa, Mirasi, Isai Vellalar and others). Each state below lists its signature instruments; names in bold have their own entries in Part 2. Sources: B. C. Deva (1978), the Sangeet Natak Akademi collections and state cultural departments. See also: MUS-02 (folk music of India).

  • Rajasthan: kamaicha, ravanhatha, morchang, algoza (and the satara double flute of Barmer), khartal, sarangi (sindhi, gujratan and jogiya), bhapang (Alwar's Mewati Jogis), nagara, chang, mashak, pungi (Kalbeliya), dholak; the Manganiyar and Langa musicians of Jaisalmer, Barmer and Jodhpur; the Bhopas of Pabuji ki phad.
  • Punjab: dhol, tumbi, algoza, chimta, sarangi, dhadd (small hourglass drum of the dhadi ballad singers), rabab and taus (Sikh kirtan heritage), bugchu and kato (folk clappers).
  • Haryana: been, dhol, nagada, dhapli (frame drum of the ragini singers), khartal.
  • Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh: santoor, rabab, tumbaknari (clay goblet drum of Kashmiri wedding songs), noet (clay pot), sarangi; Ladakh's daman (drum) and surna (shawm).
  • Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand: karnal, ransingha, dhol-damau (the drum pair of hill rituals), hudka, mashakbeen, turhi; the Dhol Sagar drumming tradition of Garhwal.
  • Uttar Pradesh and Delhi: shehnai (Banaras), tabla (Delhi, Lucknow, Farukhabad and Banaras gharanas), pakhawaj, sitar and sarod (Delhi and Lucknow courts), nagara (Braj), dholak; makers in Delhi and Lucknow.
  • Bihar and Jharkhand: mandar (Jharkhand clay drum), nagara, dhak, banam, bamboo flutes of the Santal, Oraon and Munda; jhanj cymbals.

  • West Bengal: ektara (gopichand), dotara, khamak (the Baul singers), dhak (Durga Puja), khol (kirtan), esraj (Rabindra Sangeet), sarod (the Maihar tradition took deep root in Calcutta); Kolkata's sitar and tanpura makers.
  • Odisha: mardala (Odissi), gini cymbals, khol, ghanta, changu (frame drum), bell-metal from Kantilo; temple ensembles of Puri.
  • Assam: dhol (Bihu), pepa (buffalo-horn pipe of Bihu), gogona (bamboo jaw harp), toka, taal (cymbals), khol of Sattriya music, bahi (flute).
  • Manipur: pung, pena, the large cymbals of cymbal cholom, the Nata Sankirtana tradition (UNESCO 2013).
  • Meghalaya, Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal, Tripura, Sikkim: the Khasi duitara (lute) and ksing (drum); Naga log drums; the Mizo khuang (drum) and gongs; the Tripuri sumui (flute); Buddhist ritual horns and drums in Sikkim and Arunachal. (Each needs a local-source check before its full page.)

  • Gujarat: dhol (garba), jodiya pava (Kutch double flute), jantar (stick zither of Kutch), ravanhatha, bhungal (long brass horn of the Bhavai theatre), manjira.
  • Maharashtra: dhol-tasha (Pune), halgi, dimdi, tuntune (one-string folk instrument of the tamasha and gondhal), sambal (drum pair of the Gondhal ritual), dholki (Lavani), harmonium (natya sangeet); Miraj sitar and tanpura makers (GI tag, 2024).
  • Goa: ghumot (heritage instrument, 2019), madlem and tasso; Goan musicians who shaped Bombay film orchestras (violin, trumpet, saxophone).
  • Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh: the bana fiddle of the Gond Pardhan bards; tambura of the Pandavani singers (Teejan Bai); mandar, nagada, timki; bamboo flutes of the Bhil.

  • Tamil Nadu: nadaswaram and thavil (temple music), mridangam, Saraswati veena (Thanjavur, GI), ghatam (Manamadurai), kanjira, morsing, parai, urumi, udukkai (hourglass drum), thappu; the ancient yazh.
  • Kerala: chenda, maddalam, edakka, timila, kombu, kuzhal, elathalam, mizhavu (Koodiyattam); the panchavadyam and chenda melam of Thrissur Pooram.
  • Karnataka: Saraswati veena (Mysore court tradition), nadaswaram, dollu, chande and maddale (Yakshagana), kinnari, tamate (frame drum).
  • Andhra Pradesh and Telangana: Bobbili veena (GI), dappu, kinnari (Telangana bards), the tambura and gummeta drums of Burra Katha storytelling, Oggu katha drums.

sections.title: Asia and the Middle East
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-16. The great classical traditions of Asia each built their own orchestras: gamelan, gagaku, Chinese silk-and-bamboo, maqam ensembles. See also: MUS-04.
  • INS-16.1 South Asia beyond India: Pakistan (sitar, sarangi, tabla, alghoza, benju, suroz fiddle of Balochistan, the harmonium of qawwali); Bangladesh (dotara, ektara, khol); Nepal (sarangi of the Gandharva, madal, panche baja wedding band); Sri Lanka (geta bera, yak bera, thammattama); Bhutan (dramnyen lute); Afghanistan (rubab, dutar, zerbaghali, tula flute).
  • INS-16.2 China: guqin, guzheng, pipa, erhu, dizi, sheng, suona, yangqin, xun, bianzhong; the Chinese orchestra (formed in the 20th century); the eight-material bayin (INS-03).
  • INS-16.3 Japan: koto, shamisen, shakuhachi, taiko, biwa, shō, hichiriki, ryūteki (the last three in gagaku court music, among the oldest orchestral music still played).
  • INS-16.4 Korea: gayageum, geomungo (six strings, struck with a stick), haegeum, piri, daegeum, janggu, buk; samul nori percussion quartet (1978).
  • INS-16.5 South-East Asia: gamelan (Indonesia), angklung, kulintang (Philippines), Thai piphat ensemble (ranat, khong wong, pi), Lao khaen, Vietnamese đàn bầu and đàn tranh, Burmese saung-gauk and the hsaing waing drum-circle ensemble, Cambodian pinpeat.
  • INS-16.6 Central Asia and Mongolia: dombra, komuz, dutar, tanbur, doira (frame drum), morin khuur, and Tuvan throat singing with the igil fiddle.
  • INS-16.7 Middle East and Turkey: oud, qanun, ney, darbuka, riq, daf, santur, tar, setar, kamancheh (Iran; UNESCO 2017 with Azerbaijan), bağlama, kemençe, zurna and davul, duduk (Armenia), shofar, mijwiz, rababa (Bedouin).

sections.title: Europe
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-17. Europe built the orchestra, the piano and the guitar, but it is also a continent of folk instruments. See also: MUS-05.
  • INS-17.1 The orchestra: strings (violin, viola, cello, double bass), woodwinds (flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon), brass (horn, trumpet, trombone, tuba), percussion (timpani and others), harp, keyboard. The modern symphony orchestra took shape between Haydn (1760s) and Berlioz and Wagner (19th century).
  • INS-17.2 British Isles: harp (Ireland, Wales), uilleann pipes, Highland bagpipe, bodhrán, tin whistle, fiddle, concertina, brass bands of northern England.
  • INS-17.3 Iberia: classical and flamenco guitar, castanets, cajón (in flamenco since the 1970s, via Paco de Lucía), gaita, Portuguese guitar, cavaquinho.
  • INS-17.4 Central and western Europe: accordion, alphorn, zither, hurdy-gurdy, musette, organ, harpsichord, recorder; violin making at Cremona (UNESCO 2012), Mittenwald and Mirecourt.
  • INS-17.5 Nordic and Baltic: hardanger fiddle, nyckelharpa, kantele, kanklės, the Sámi drum.
  • INS-17.6 Eastern Europe and the Balkans: balalaika, domra, gusli, cimbalom, kobza and bandura (Ukraine), tambura (Balkans), gusle, kaval, gaida, tapan; Romanian nai.
  • INS-17.7 Mediterranean: mandolin, zampogna, launeddas, bouzouki, lyra (Crete), tamburello.

sections.title: The Americas and the Caribbean
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-18. The Americas mix Indigenous, African and European traditions, which produced the banjo, the steelpan and the drum kit. See also: MUS-06.
  • INS-18.1 Indigenous instruments: the Plains flute, powwow drum, rattles and water drums of North America; Andean quena, siku, charango (post-contact), bombo; Mesoamerican clay whistles and the teponaztli slit drum; Amazonian flutes and panpipes.
  • INS-18.2 USA and Canada: banjo, fiddle, harmonica, steel-string and electric guitar, pedal steel, Dobro, drum kit, saxophone and trumpet in jazz, the Hammond organ in gospel, the Appalachian dulcimer.
  • INS-18.3 Mexico and Central America: mariachi (violins, trumpets, vihuela, guitarrón), marimba (Guatemala, Chiapas), jarana (son jarocho).
  • INS-18.4 The Caribbean: steelpan (Trinidad and Tobago), conga, bongo, timbales, güiro, claves, tres (Cuba), cuatro (Puerto Rico), the tambora and accordion of Dominican merengue.
  • INS-18.5 South America: bandoneón (tango), berimbau (a musical bow of capoeira, Brazil), pandeiro, cuíca, surdo, cavaquinho, the Venezuelan cuatro and harp, the Colombian gaita flute and tiple, the Peruvian cajón; Venezuela's El Sistema youth orchestras (founded 1975 by José Antonio Abreu).

sections.title: Africa and Oceania
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-19. Africa is the homeland of many instrument ideas: the harp-lute, the lamellophone, the talking drum and the xylophone with gourds. Oceania gave the world the didgeridoo and the ukulele's island home. See also: MUS-07.
  • INS-19.1 West Africa: kora, balafon, djembe, dùndún (talking drum), ngoni, xalam, akonting (Gambia, a banjo ancestor), goje (fiddle), shekere, udu; griots (jeli) as hereditary keepers.
  • INS-19.2 North and East Africa: oud, darbuka, gimbri (Gnawa), imzad (Tuareg), krar, begena and masenqo (Ethiopia), the nyatiti lyre (Kenya), adungu harp and amadinda xylophone (Uganda).
  • INS-19.3 Central and Southern Africa: mbira, likembe, timbila, marimba, the uhadi and other musical bows (South Africa), the vuvuzela; the valiha (Madagascar).
  • INS-19.4 Oceania: didgeridoo (yidaki) and clapsticks (Aboriginal Australia), bullroarer, Māori taonga pūoro (kōauau flute, pūtōrino, pūkāea horn), Hawaiian pahu, ipu gourd drum, ʻukulele and steel guitar, the slit drums of Fiji (lali), Vanuatu and Papua New Guinea (garamut), and the PNG hourglass kundu drum (on the national emblem).

sections.title: Great inventions and journeys
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-21. Some instruments changed the world's music. Here are their stories in brief; each becomes a full page.
  • INS-21.1 The veena's journey: from the Vedic vana and the arched-harp vina of early sculpture, to the stick-zither rudra veena of medieval North India, to the fretted lute of the South (the Saraswati veena took its present form in Thanjavur around the 17th century, credited to the court of Raghunatha Nayak). One name, three kinds of instrument.
  • INS-21.2 The Cremona miracle: Andrea Amati, then the Guarneri and Stradivari families, set the violin's shape for 400 years. Blind tests (Claudia Fritz and colleagues, 2012 and 2014) found that top soloists often could not tell Stradivaris from good new violins, and some preferred the new ones.
  • INS-21.3 The piano's rise: Cristofori's hammer action; the Viennese and English pianos of Mozart and Beethoven; the iron frame; the piano as the centre of 19th-century homes; the upright in Indian homes and churches.
  • INS-21.4 Adolphe Sax and the saxophone: designed in the 1840s to bridge woodwind and brass in military bands; nearly forgotten, then reborn in jazz; Kadri Gopalnath's Carnatic sax.
  • INS-21.5 The harmonium in India: from French parlour to Indian floor; banned by All India Radio (1940–71) after critics, Rabindranath Tagore among them, argued it could not play Indian microtones; today indispensable.
  • INS-21.6 The tabla's birth: legends credit Amir Khusrau; historians date the tabla to the 18th century, perhaps developed from the pakhawaj and the dholak in Delhi (Sudhar Khan and Siddhar Khan Dhadi are traditional founders of the Delhi gharana).
  • INS-21.7 The electric guitar: from loudness for big bands to the voice of rock; the solid body; distortion as art.
  • INS-21.8 Synthesizers and drum machines: from laboratories to bedrooms; the TR-808 was a commercial flop before it shaped hip-hop.
  • INS-21.9 Digital and AI instruments: software instruments, sample libraries of Indian instruments, AI-generated sound, and debates about the future of hand-made instruments.
  • INS-21.10 Instruments lost and revived: the yazh (reconstruction efforts in Tamil Nadu), the surbahar's decline, the baroque revival of the harpsichord and viols, endangered folk instruments of India and their revival through fairs and festivals (Rajasthan International Folk Festival, Jodhpur).

parts.title: The Craft: Acoustics, Making, Care and Tuning
parts.intro: About this Part. How instruments work as physics, how they are made, and how to look after and tune them. See also: TEC (audio technology), the Curriculum Index (SNT: sound and waves).

sections.title: The physics of sound in instruments
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-26. Every instrument has three parts: an exciter (bow, breath, finger, stick), a vibrator (string, reed, lips, skin, solid body) and a resonator (body, tube, gourd, room). Change any of them and the sound changes.
  • INS-26.1 Frequency, pitch and the octave: doubling the frequency gives the octave (Sa to the upper Sa); humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, less with age.
  • INS-26.2 Strings: Mersenne's laws (INS-00.02); harmonics touched lightly at half, third or quarter length; the "stick-slip" motion of the bow (Hermann von Helmholtz, 1860s).
  • INS-26.3 Air columns: open tubes (flute) give all harmonics; tubes closed at one end (clarinet) mostly odd ones; conical bores (oboe, saxophone, shehnai) behave like open tubes; finger holes and valves change the effective length.
  • INS-26.4 Membranes and plates: drum skins and gongs vibrate in complex patterns (Chladni figures, shown with sand by Ernst Chladni, 1787); C. V. Raman's work on the harmonic Indian drums (1920) and on the veena and tanpura bridge.
  • INS-26.5 Resonance and the body: soundboards, gourds and shells amplify; sympathetic strings resonate by themselves (INS-00.05).
  • INS-26.6 Timbre: overtone spectrum plus envelope (INS-00.03); formants explain why a sarangi sounds vocal.
  • INS-26.7 Tuning systems: just intonation (pure ratios), Pythagorean tuning, equal temperament (12 equal semitones, standard in Western music since the 19th century), and the Indian shruti (22 microtonal positions in the old texts); the tanpura and harmonium debate (INS-21.5).
  • INS-26.8 Concert pitch: A = 440 Hz was agreed at a 1939 London conference and set as ISO 16 in 1975; Baroque groups often use 415 Hz; Indian music uses a movable Sa chosen to suit the singer or instrument.
  • INS-26.9 Room acoustics: reverberation time; why the same instrument sounds different in a hall, a temple courtyard and a studio (MUS-20.7).

sections.title: Making instruments: luthiery and materials
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-27. Instrument making is called luthiery for strings (from "lute") and has its own crafts for drums, winds and brass. In India most makers learn in family workshops. See also: INS-23 (makers).

  • Woods: spruce (soundboards: light and stiff), maple (violin backs), rosewood and ebony (fingerboards, backs), mahogany, cedar; Indian tun (red cedar, sitars and sarangis), teak (sarods), jackfruit (veena, mridangam), sheesham (tabla, khartal), bamboo (flutes); pernambuco (the best bows, now endangered).
  • Gourds and shells: the tumba gourds of sitars and tanpuras grown around Pandharpur (Maharashtra), coconut shells (ravanhatha, pena), calabash (kora, balafon).
  • Skins and gut: goat, sheep, buffalo and cow skins for drums; gut strings (sheep intestine) for old violins and sarangis; ethical and caste questions attach to skin work (INS-23.6).
  • Metals: brass, bronze and bell metal (kansa, about 78 per cent copper and 22 per cent tin in many Indian traditions), steel strings, silver flutes, cymbal alloys (B20 bronze).
  • Synthetics: nylon (guitar strings since the 1940s, Albert Augustine with Segovia), plastic drumheads (Remo, 1957), carbon fibre (cellos and bows), 3D-printed instruments.

  • Bowed and plucked strings: carving the top and back, bending the sides, setting the neck, varnish (the "Stradivari varnish" myth); the sitar's gourd joined to a tun neck, frets tied with gut, the jawari shaped by hand (INS-00.05).
  • Drums: shell turning or carving, skin preparation, lacing (baddhi), the multiple-layer syahi of the tabla applied in many thin coats and polished with a stone.
  • Wind: bamboo selection and heat-drilling of bansuri holes; reed making for oboe, shehnai (from palm leaf or pala grass) and nadaswaram (from naanal reed); brass bending and valve fitting.
  • Clay and metal idiophones: the ghatam's clay mixed with metal filings and fired; gongs hammered and tuned; bells cast by the lost-wax or sand method.
  • Craft clusters and GI tags: Cremona, Mirecourt, Mittenwald (violins); Paracho (guitars); Miraj (sitar, tanpura), Thanjavur and Bobbili (veena), Manamadurai (ghatam), Pilibhit (bansuri), Kolkata and Varanasi (sitar, tabla).

sections.title: Care, repair and tuning
sections.html:
Before you start — INS-28. Most damage to instruments comes from heat, damp and dryness. Wood and skin move with the weather.
  • INS-28.1 Climate: keep wooden instruments at moderate humidity (roughly 40–60 per cent) and away from direct sun, heaters and car boots; monsoon care for tabla and sitar (silica gel, a cloth cover, never sealed plastic in damp).
  • INS-28.2 Strings and bows: change strings regularly; wipe off rosin; have bows re-haired; loosen the bow after playing.
  • INS-28.3 Drums: tune tabla with a hammer on the gatta (wooden blocks) and the rim; keep the syahi dry; mridangam left head paste removed after playing.
  • INS-28.4 Winds and brass: dry and swab after playing; reeds stored flat; valve oil; bansuri oiled lightly to prevent cracks.
  • INS-28.5 Pianos and harmoniums: tune a piano once or twice a year; harmonium reeds kept dust-free; old ivory keys are legal to keep but trade rules apply (INS-33.5).
  • INS-28.6 Tuning tools: tuning fork, electronic tuners and apps, the tanpura or electronic shruti as reference, and the ear above all.
  • INS-28.7 Repair and the repairer's craft: when to visit a luthier; the honest value of an old instrument.
